figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: We introduce Scientist World. Each research paper becomes an executable environment, where an AI-Scientist ’s Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI) is above zero when its method improves on the paper’s reproduced one. We test how well AI-Scientists improve existing research (left) and innovate new research from scratch (right). We show the best model of each lab plus the next best overall; full leaderboards are in Figure 12.
figures.headline: The best model from each lab is scored on improving existing papers and on innovating from scratch, with zero matching the reproduced method.
citing_sentences: Building from high-quality papers, we first release 1,000 environments, and it keeps growing with the literature (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Where Scientist World stands. Prior AI-Scientist environments sit on the trade-off surface we describe; Scientist World reaches the corner where scale, evolve, and execution meet.
figures.headline: Scientist World reaches the corner where scale, evolving, and execution-grounded properties meet, unlike prior environments.
citing_sentences: Scientist World holds three at once (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Scientist World is three things at once. One set of environments, grown from real papers, serves all three.
figures.headline: One set of environments built from real papers serves as a benchmark, a dataset, and a gym.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Builders turn a paper into an environment. Construction runs like an assembly line: a published paper enters at one end, and a reusable research environment leaves the other. Specialized builders take turns on a single shared workspace, each refining what the previous one built and offloading heavy computation to a shared cluster. A quality gate guards the line, sending unfinished work back for another pass, so only what clears verification is accepted.
figures.headline: Builders convert each paper through repeated agent iterations on one shared workspace, with a quality gate sending unfinished work back.
citing_sentences: We convert each paper through a sequence of agent iterations on one shared workspace (Figure 4).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Using compute. A builder submits a job to the shared pool, sleeps, and is woken with the logs; its GPU budget is enforced outside the loop.
figures.headline: Builders submit compute jobs to a shared pool and wait until woken with logs, with GPU budget enforced outside the loop.
citing_sentences: All experiments run on a shared pool of compute machines (Figure 5), described in §A with details.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Anatomy of an environment. A produced environment is a single self-contained workspace, laid out so the problem stays separate from the solution. The briefing, data, and scoring fix what to solve and how it is judged without referring to any one method, which keeps the task open to future approaches and stops a score from depending on the implementation. The method is the paper’s source method reproduced, and the scores it reaches are the reference we compare against, so a new method’s final score is the improvement it makes over them.
figures.headline: One produced environment is a self-contained workspace that separates the problem, data, and scoring from the source method.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 walks through one produced environment in full.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Selecting 1,000 papers from 124,816 indexed. In a first pass (a), we drop papers that are low quality or are mainly a type of theory, a benchmark, a dataset, or a single finding, which leaves 21,354. In (b), we look at these more closely and favor work that is both high quality and compute-friendly, keeping the best 1,000. In (c), we check the result: the papers we picked (blue) are clearly stronger and more reproducible than the pool we started from (grey).
figures.headline: Screening drops 124,816 indexed papers to 21,354, then keeps the 1,000 that are high quality and compute-friendly.
citing_sentences: Our selection pipeline keeps papers that are worth building under budget (Figure 7).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: The environment composition. The produced environments can be categorized into eight areas.
figures.headline: The 1,000 environments are spread across eight areas.
citing_sentences: We first release 1,000 environments spread across eight areas (Figure 8).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: An example environment. This environment turns a Transformer architecture paper into a constrained improvement task: raise ImageNet accuracy without changing scale, pretraining, or data. The scripts make the task runnable, the source and baseline implementations anchor the comparison, and the scoring matrix defines progress as weighted improvement over the reproduced source method.
figures.headline: An example Transformer task raises ImageNet accuracy without changing scale, pretraining, or data, scored against the reproduced source method.
citing_sentences: Figure 9 shows one environment end to end.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Environments’ openness. From fully prescribed (0) to fully open (100).
figures.headline: Every area covers nearly the full openness range from 0 to 100, so freedom depends on the task rather than its area.
citing_sentences: We find that every area covers nearly the whole range (Figure 10): the level of freedom of an environment depends on the task itself, not on where in the world it sits.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: What the environments ask for. Each task names, in its own words, what should get better.
figures.headline: Each environment states in its own words what should get better, collected across the 1,000 tasks.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Leaderboards. Mean FNI by model in improve mode (top) and innovate mode (bottom), averaged over visible and held-out splits. Zero matches the reproduced source method; higher is better. Improve mode gives models the source method, while innovate mode requires them to design from scratch. We use xhigh effort for all models.
figures.headline: Fable 5 leads improve mode, while Fable 5.1 and Fable 5 take the top two places in innovate mode.
citing_sentences: In the result, the two modes show different strengths across models (Figure 12): Fable 5 is the strongest at improving existing methods, while Fable 5.1 and Fable 5 take the top two places at designing new methods from scratch.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: The two abilities are loosely tied. Each model’s rank at improving against its rank at innovating.
figures.headline: Model ranks at improving and at innovating are only loosely related, so the two abilities are treated as distinct.
citing_sentences: Instead, the relationship is loose (Figure 13).

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Effort versus outcome, and research quality. (a) each run’s score against the compute hours (top) and agent turns (bottom) behind it, pooling both modes; effort explains almost none of the variance in score ($R^{2}=0.00$, $0.02$). (b) research quality by dimension, judged apart from the score. Newest model per family, colored by provider.
figures.headline: Effort explains at most 0.02 of score variance; judged research quality tracks score with correlation 0.89.
citing_sentences: Compute hours and agent turns explain almost none of the variance in scores ($R^{2}\leq 0.02$, Figure 14a; turns are our provider-agnostic proxy for model-side effort, since token counts may not be available).
These ratings track the models’ actual scores almost exactly ($\rho=0.89$, Figure 14b): the models that win are the ones doing better research, not the ones trying hardest.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Raised in the world. Median held-out FNI of each stage’s ideas, implemented identically; after GRPO it reaches the frontier cohort’s anchor.
figures.headline: Median held-out Frontier-Normalized Improvement rises from 41 for the base scientist to 84 after supervised fine-tuning and 106 after policy optimization.
citing_sentences: The median implemented idea scores 41 FNI from the base scientist, 84 after SFT, and 106 after GRPO (Figure 15); the mean rises from 51 to 90.
It records how the corpus is counted, how the training data and configuration are derived from it, and the held-out protocol behind Figure 15.
The gym result of Figure 15 scores ideas, not the idea generator’s own coding.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: System design overview. Hive supplies execution capacity for CPU and GPU jobs; Nexus accounts for the budget and resource boundary of each attempt; Swarm maintains one paper-level trajectory across roles, restarts, and handoffs; and Workers connect different agent scaffolds through the same system interface. Together, these layers let many agents iterate on open-ended papers while preserving the evidence, budget state, and handoff context.
figures.headline: Four layers, Hive, Nexus, Swarm, and Worker, keep compute, budget, paper trajectories, and agent interfaces separate.
citing_sentences: Figure 16 summarizes these layers.

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Hive execution overview. A job request enters Hive with a command, resource target, working directory, and time limit. Admission queues the request, dispatch routes it to test, CPU, or GPU capacity, and monitor records the return code, runtime, and logs that form the job record.
figures.headline: A job request is admitted, dispatched to test, CPU, or GPU capacity, and recorded with return code, runtime, and logs.
citing_sentences: Figure 17 shows the execution path inside Hive.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: Nexus operations overview. Nexus stores the job, project, budget, and review state needed to translate agent requests into Hive actions and to translate Hive execution evidence back into agent decisions.
figures.headline: Nexus translates agent requests into Hive actions and translates Hive execution evidence back into agent decisions.
citing_sentences: The operations view in Figure 18 shows these exchanges: agents submit or review jobs through Nexus, and Nexus communicates between infrastructures and agents.

figures.label: Figure 19
figures.caption: A Nexus project turns resource policy into explicit accept/reject decisions. The example shows how budget, concurrency, and allowed resource pools gate agent requests before they reach Hive.
figures.headline: A Nexus project rejects requests that exceed the remaining budget or concurrency, or that request a disallowed resource pool.
citing_sentences: The project-level example in Figure 19 makes the gate concrete: a request can be rejected because it exceeds the remaining budget or concurrency capacity, or requests a resource pool outside the given policy.

figures.label: Figure 20
figures.caption: Swarm coordination overview. Swarm drives a pool of paper workspaces in parallel. Each paper moves through an ordered role workflow—reproduce, design, package, verify—whose transitions are driven by wake events: worker start, job submit, job update, validation failure, and role transition. Progress is graded against a milestone ladder, from none up to full reproduction, and the milestone gate decides whether a paper’s artifact is accepted.
figures.headline: Each paper moves through reproduce, design, package, and verify roles, gated by a milestone ladder that decides acceptance.
citing_sentences: Figure 20 shows the end-to-end path: a pool of paper workspaces, each driven through an ordered role workflow under a milestone gate, ending in an artifact that is either accepted or set aside.

figures.label: Figure 21
figures.caption: Swarm workflow stages. The standard workflow expands reproduction, design, packaging, and verification into repeated builder passes; each row carries the model profile, gate, GPU budget, and possible revert target.
figures.headline: The standard workflow repeats reproduction, design, packaging, and verification passes, each with a gate and a possible revert target.
citing_sentences: The standard workflow is an ordered list of stage rows (Figure 21).

figures.label: Figure 22
figures.caption: Worker runtime overview. Different agent scaffolds connect through one uniform turn interface. Worker runs the agent under a container runtime with capped resources and a read-only validator, cycling through a turn loop of render prompt, agent acts, and submit jobs. Each turn ends by selecting the next action in action.yaml, which the system reads before waking the agent for the following turn.
figures.headline: Different agent scaffolds connect through one uniform turn interface inside a capped container with a read-only validator.
citing_sentences: Figure 22 shows this path: heterogeneous scaffolds enter through one uniform turn interface, run inside a constrained container, and end each turn by writing an action.yaml that wakes the system for the next turn.

figures.label: Figure 23
figures.caption: The action.yaml that ends a turn. The agent writes it to request the next job or to stop, and the system reads it after every turn.
figures.headline: Each turn ends by writing action.yaml, which requests the next job or stops the agent.
citing_sentences: The agent ends a turn by writing one file, action.yaml, that states its decision, shown in Figure 23.

figures.label: Figure 24
figures.caption: Builder overview. From a paper (in PDF and Markdown) and an empty starter workspace, builders build a reusable environment along three tracks: a problem definition that states the task and its constraints without leaking a solution, a reproduction of the paper’s method whose code and experiments recover the central claim, and an evaluation harness with visible and hidden slices that turns outputs into scores.
figures.headline: Builders turn a paper and an empty workspace into a problem definition, a reproduced method, and an evaluation harness with visible and hidden slices.
citing_sentences: Figure 24 gives the overview: from a paper and an empty workspace, builders produce a reusable environment across problem definition, method reproduction, and evaluation.

figures.label: Figure 25
figures.caption: The agent workspace. A single directory holds the paper and briefing, the reproduced method and baselines, the data and evaluator, the scoring contract, the run scripts and environment, and the root-level record and validation files. Each directory has a single responsibility, which keeps the problem separated from the solution, lets the workspace rebuild and rerun from a fresh clone, and preserves a record of how the reproduction was produced.
figures.headline: The agent workspace keeps the paper, reproduced method, evaluator, scoring contract, and run records in separate directories.
citing_sentences: The layout shown in Figure 25 is designed to prevent these failures.
The few excerpts below come from the produced workspace; layout follows Figure 25.

figures.label: Figure 26
figures.caption: The scoring contract, held in two files. scoring/reference.json fixes the weights, metric directions, coefficients, and the paper’s reported numbers; scoring/scores.json holds the numbers the reproduction actually produced, under the same keys.
figures.headline: The scoring contract stores fixed weights and reported numbers in one file and produced numbers in another under the same keys.
citing_sentences: Figure 26 shows the two files side by side.

figures.label: Figure 27
figures.caption: Each design choice targets a concrete failure mode. The workspace is structured to avoid solution leakage, method-coupled scoring, unrebuildable dependencies, evaluator overfitting, and unsupported claims.
figures.headline: Each workspace design choice targets a named failure mode, such as solution leakage or evaluator overfitting.
citing_sentences: Figure 27 collects them: the design decision, the failure it prevents, and where it lives.

figures.label: Figure 28
figures.caption: Screening preserves nearly all unique papers before deeper analysis. Counts are computed from the selection snapshot used by the export. Shares after the unique-index row use 124,816 as the denominator.
figures.headline: Screening keeps nearly all unique papers before deeper analysis, with shares computed against 124,816.
citing_sentences: Figure 28 reports how many papers survive each screening stage from this pool onward.

figures.label: Figure 29
figures.caption: The source pool is largest in cs.AI and cs.LG before deduplication. These are category-listing records before ID-level deduplication; a single paper can contribute to multiple rows.
figures.headline: The source pool is largest in cs.AI and cs.LG before deduplication, since one paper can appear under several categories.
citing_sentences: We restrict the source categories to cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.AI, and cs.LG (Figure 29), then deduplicate by arXiv ID because the same paper can appear under more than one category.

figures.label: Figure 30
figures.caption: Fast screens keep broad coverage while identifying metric-method papers as the dominant type. The left side summarizes 123,980 fast quality scores; the right side summarizes 124,018 fast paper-type labels.
figures.headline: Fast screens cover a broad range of quality scores, with metric-method papers as the dominant paper type.
citing_sentences: Figure 30 reports the full quality-score and paper-type distributions.

figures.label: Figure 31
figures.caption: Structured-analysis score distributions across the 21,354 analyzed papers. Each panel gives the share of papers at each integer score from 0 to 10: the five reproduction-difficulty sub-scores (coding, compute, time to run, data or model, and overall), and the paper-level quality and problem-novelty scores. Dashed lines mark the means. Difficulty scores concentrate in the low-to-middle range, while quality and problem novelty center higher.
figures.headline: Reproduction-difficulty scores concentrate in the low-to-middle range, while quality and problem-novelty scores center higher.
citing_sentences: Figure 31 shows how these scores are distributed across the analyzed papers.

figures.label: Figure 32
figures.caption: Feasibility filters reduce 21,354 analyzed papers to 8,987 candidates. The feasible candidates are ranked by quality-feasibility utility before the final category-balanced selection.
figures.headline: Feasibility filters reduce 21,354 analyzed papers to 8,987 candidates before the final category-balanced selection.
citing_sentences: The fast type label guides this stage but does not filter it; the decisive type filter uses the structured analysis’s own classification and appears as the first drops in Figure 32.
The filtering counts in Figure 32 are sequential counts from the exported snapshot, each paper attributed to its first rejecting rule.

figures.label: Figure 33
figures.caption: Temperature-balanced sampling keeps large areas prominent while preserving smaller categories. The final 1,000-paper selection is sampled from 8,987 feasible candidates across 18 canonical categories.
figures.headline: Temperature-balanced sampling keeps large categories prominent while preserving smaller ones, selecting 1,000 from 8,987 candidates.
citing_sentences: Figure 33 shows the candidate pool and selected count for each canonical category.

figures.label: Figure 34
figures.caption: What environments ask, and the work it takes. Each environment states what should get better and what work that takes; phrases are grouped into families that emerge from data; ribbon mass is the share of environments.
figures.headline: Environments state what should improve and the work required, grouped into families that emerge from the data.
citing_sentences: Figure 34 reads the resulting environments in their own words: what each asks to make better, and the work delivering it requires.

figures.label: Figure 35
figures.caption: How often scientists beat the paper. Distribution of held-out improvement over the paper’s source method, per mode. Colored bars (right of zero) beat the reproduced method; the grey tail regressed. The percentage is the share of runs that improved.
figures.headline: Most runs improve on the reproduced method in both modes, with the share of improving runs marked on each panel.
citing_sentences: Figure 35 shows the distribution of held-out improvement over the paper’s source method, one panel per mode.

figures.label: Figure 36
figures.caption: Training gains carry over to held-out test. Training-phase score against held-out test score, per mode, with the $y=x$ line. Points hug the diagonal; the shaded quadrant holds the few runs that gained on training but regressed on test.
figures.headline: Training-phase gains mostly carry over to held-out test, with only a few runs gaining on training but regressing on test.
citing_sentences: Figure 36 plots one against the other.

figures.label: Figure 37
figures.caption: Effort versus outcome. Within-paper normalized score against GPU-hours (top row) and agent turns (bottom row), shown separately for the Improve and Innovate modes. Scores are min-max normalized within each (paper, mode); each line is a least-squares fit in log-effort. Every panel is flat ($|\rho|\leq 0.22$).
figures.headline: Within-paper normalized score is flat against GPU-hours and agent turns in both modes, with absolute correlation at most 0.22.
citing_sentences: Figure 37 plots each run’s within-paper normalized score against the GPU-hours it consumed and the number of turns it took, with the Improve and Innovate modes kept apart.

figures.label: Figure 38
figures.caption: Trained ideas against the base. Each of the ten held-out papers contributes one SFT and one GRPO dot, plotted against the same paper’s base idea score (displayed scaled by 100). A dot above the dashed diagonal means the trained idea beat the untrained idea on that paper.
figures.headline: Each trained idea is plotted against its base idea on ten held-out papers, with points above the diagonal marking gains.
citing_sentences: Figure 38 plots each trained idea’s score against the same paper’s base idea score, and Table 14 summarizes the distributions over the ten held-out papers.

abstract: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.

sections.body: The paper introduces Scientist World, a set of research environments built from the scientific literature. A multi-agent pipeline with no human in the loop reproduces each paper's method, designs a task with a scoring rule, packages it to run on any machine, and verifies it with independent agents. An AI-Scientist is scored by its Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI) over the human authors' method. The authors release the first 1,000 environments and describe three uses: a benchmark, a dataset of attempts, and a gym for training. The introduction claims the environments are scalable, evolving, and execution-grounded, and the later sections test these claims.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Scientist World turns 1,000 papers into executable research environments that grade AI-Scientists against the paper's human result.

sections.body: Four builder roles convert each paper into an environment on one shared workspace. The reproducer re-establishes the paper's main result. The designer writes the problem statement, fixes the task rules, and sets the source result as the bar, with a visible and a held-out evaluation set. The packager replaces local files with download scripts and declares dependencies, so a fresh clone can rebuild and rerun. The verifier audits the packaged environment as a separate role. A milestone ladder gates each iteration, and a failed gate reverts work to an earlier iteration. Scores are reported as Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI) over the source method, with the held-out slice reserved to catch shortcuts and overfitting.
sections.heading: From Papers to Environments
sections.headline: Four builder agents reproduce each paper, design a scored task, package it to run anywhere, and verify it without humans.

sections.body: The selection pipeline starts from 124,816 unique papers across fourteen months of core AI categories. Two fast screens with MiniMax M2.7 leave 21,354 papers. Detailed judgments on quality and reproduction difficulty then sample the category-balanced top 1,000. No human reviews any paper. Table 1 reports a median of 76 compute jobs and 0.4 GPU-hours per paper, with 2,286 GPU-hours in total. Each paper goes through a nine-iteration workflow. Acceptance rests on four checks: reproduction fidelity, baseline separation, iterative cross-checking, and independent verification. The authors report that every area covers nearly the full openness range from 0 to 100.
sections.heading: Scientist World
sections.headline: Selection narrows 124,816 papers to 1,000 that build under a compute budget, with a median of 0.4 GPU-hours per paper.

sections.body: Each model attempts ten lower-compute environments in two modes: improve, which starts from the reproduced source method, and innovate, which starts with no source code. Zero FNI matches the source method, and AI-Scientists beat it in 84% of improve and 74% of innovate attempts. Fable 5 is strongest at improving, while Fable 5.1 and Fable 5 take the top two places at innovating. Compute hours and agent turns explain almost none of the variance in score, and judged research quality tracks score at rho 0.89. A Qwen3-8B scientist, supervised fine-tuned and then trained with GRPO on scored ideas, raises the median implemented idea from 41 to 106 FNI.
sections.heading: Scientists in the World
sections.headline: AI-Scientists beat the paper's reproduced method in 84% of improve attempts and 74% of innovate attempts.

sections.body: The background traces automated discovery from symbolic regression and robot scientists through program search to tool-augmented agents that run experiments and draft papers. Evaluation work covers general agent benchmarks, machine-learning experimentation, scientific reasoning, and paper reproduction. The authors note that these suites are almost always fixed and hand-curated, and that agent evaluations can confound cost, leak through weak holdouts, and reward shortcuts. Concurrent work turns papers into tasks but curates them by hand, which does not scale. The paper's contribution is to treat construction itself as the object: it selects papers at scale and refactors each into a reproduce-then-improve environment.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: Prior AI-Scientist work either builds better scientists or uses fixed, hand-curated suites that can leak and reward shortcuts.

sections.body: The conclusion states that 1,000 papers become runnable, scored environments, and that the collection grows with the literature rather than with annotation effort. It presents the same environments as a way to measure current AI-Scientists and train future ones. It also cautions that each environment is a scaled-down paper and that each score reflects one contingent trajectory. The loop of proposing, executing, and updating inside the world is described as just beginning. The section then thanks colleagues and acknowledges Princeton Research Computing resources.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The paper argues the environments can keep growing with the literature, though each score reflects one contingent trajectory.

sections.body: The appendix describes the builder system: Hive for compute, Nexus for per-attempt budgets, Swarm for paper-level coordination, and Worker for agent interfaces. It then covers builder design choices, the agent workspace layout, paper selection counts, the evaluation protocol and scoring, analysis of how often scientists beat papers and whether gains generalize, the experimental setup, the trace corpus, training data, held-out evaluation, a worked Dynamic Tanh example environment, and agent prompts. Most of this content is operational detail behind the main results.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers the builder system, paper selection, evaluation protocol and analysis, experimental setup, dataset, and prompts.
